claims.text: Spotify has merged more than 2.5 million automated maintenance PRs via Fleet Management, the vast majority auto-merged with no human in the loop.
Spotify's Honk background coding agent runs Claude using the Agent SDK, wrapped inside Spotify's own harness and deployed in Kubernetes pods so many sessions can be scheduled concurrently.
Honk has access to a set of trusted tools, including the ability to run builds in Spotify's CI environment across multiple operating systems to verify its changes are correct.
Spotify's most recent Java migration across its backend services took three days using Fleet Management and Honk.
Spotify states that migrations that used to take hundreds of teams weeks or months can now be done by a single engineer in a few days.

Spotify built Fleet Management (executed by a system called Fleetshift) after noticing its production codebase was growing seven times faster than the number of engineers, with migrations the top source of developer frustration.

Fleet Management's deterministic scripts hit breaking point on complex changes such as replacing API calls and refactoring usage patterns, which motivated using an LLM-based agent (Honk) for code modifications.
In the Fleet Management integration, Fleetshift handles orchestration (identifying targets, scheduling changes, tracking progress) while Honk performs the actual code modifications.
Spotify reports more than 99% of engineers use AI coding tools weekly, 94% report higher productivity, and pull request frequency rose 76%.
Spotify says agent performance is measurably worse in its more fragmented codebases, and that consistent code (e.g., standardized backend services) lets Claude perform significantly better.

Spotify uses Soundcheck and golden state standards combined with static analysis and linting as guardrails, so the agent gets immediate lint feedback and self-corrects when using non-optimal patterns.
Spotify exposes Backstage capabilities (component ownership, documentation, contacting the owning team on Slack) to agents as MCPs and command-line tools.
Honk is available over Slack, and Honk v2 adds shared multiplayer agent sessions, team projects, and orchestration through Chirp.

In a Honk dataset-migration case study, Spotify needed to migrate about 1,800 direct downstream data pipelines in six months across three frameworks (BigQuery Runner, dbt, and Scala-based Scio), estimated at about 10 engineering weeks if done manually.
Spotify rolled out 240 automated migration PRs via Fleetshift for the dataset migration, saving an estimated 10 engineering weeks.
Spotify used Backstage endpoint lineage and Codesearch plugins to identify downstream consumers and target repositories for the dataset migration.

At the time of the dataset migration, Honk had no access to Claude skills or custom configurability, a deliberate guardrail, so prompts had to be fully comprehensive since the agent could not use MCPs or read external docs.
Spotify dropped Scio migrations in this effort because pipelines varied too much between teams to write a comprehensive prompt, while the more standardized dbt and BigQuery Runner pipelines worked.
A context file generated by having Claude repurpose a human migration guide was insufficient and led Honk to make incorrect field-mapping assumptions; making mappings explicit in tables fixed this.
Spotify instructed Honk to leave fields needing judgment calls unchanged and add comments linking to human migration guides for reviewers.
BigQuery Runner and dbt repositories rarely had build-time unit tests, so Honk's verify-and-adjust loop was unavailable and owning teams had to manually test the automated PRs before merging.
Spotify identifies the most serious failure mode of background agents as a PR that passes CI but is functionally incorrect, because it erodes trust; failing to produce a PR is a minor annoyance.
Spotify's Honk verification loops include an LLM judge that receives the proposed diff and the original prompt for evaluation.

Ramp's Inspect background coding agent runs each session in a Modal Sandbox with a full-stack dev environment (Postgres, Redis, Temporal, RabbitMQ) and integrates with Sentry, Datadog, LaunchDarkly and Temporal to verify its own work; it now writes over half of merged PRs at Ramp.

Shopify's Helix migrates React Native screens to Swift/Kotlin in small checkpoints, each passing four gates in order: CLI behavior tests, a Gemini-based UI visual review against the reference app, two context-isolated adversarial code reviewer agents that must both approve, and engineer approval.
